/library/an-evening-wind-down.html:
The last hour of the day often fills itself: one more message, one more episode, one more look at the news. A simple wind-down will not solve every sleep problem, and it is not a treatment for insomnia or for any other health condition. For many people, though, a short, repeatable routine can help the body and mind recognize that night is arriving.
MyHealth.Alberta.ca describes insomnia as trouble getting to sleep, staying asleep, or sleeping as long as you need, and notes that sleep difficulty can be linked to health problems, medicines and stressful events. If sleep has been hard for a while, a healthcare provider can help you look at the larger picture. The ideas below are everyday practices, not a personal care plan.
Keep a regular sleep schedule
One of the most useful steps in public sleep guidance is also one of the plainest: go to bed at about the same time each night and get up at about the same time each morning. MyHealth.Alberta.ca suggests keeping that schedule even when you are working on sleep, and avoiding daytime naps if they make night-time sleep harder.
A regular rising time can matter as much as a regular bedtime. If you have had a short night, it can be tempting to sleep in. A consistent morning hour, with daylight if you can get it, may help your body clock stay steadier over the following days.
Give your bedroom a clear job
MyHealth.Alberta.ca recommends using the bedroom for sleep and sex, and not reading, watching television or using your phone in bed. The idea is to keep the bed linked with rest, rather than with problem-solving, scrolling or work.
If your home does not allow a perfect setup, do what you can. A cooler, darker, quieter room is the usual aim. If noise or light is hard to control, a sleep mask or earplugs are options some people find helpful. There is no single “right” bedroom, only a space that feels as calm as your circumstances allow.
If you are still awake after a short while
Give yourself about 15 to 20 minutes to fall asleep. If you are still awake, MyHealth.Alberta.ca suggests getting out of bed and doing a quiet task until you feel sleepy again. That step is meant to keep the bed from becoming a place you associate with lying awake and watching the clock.
Choose something low-key and already familiar: folding a few clothes, reading a paper page under dim light, or sitting with a warm, non-caffeinated drink. Bright screens, exciting shows and work email tend to pull the other way.
Build a short wind-down you can repeat
A relaxing bedtime routine can help teach your body and mind that it is time to slow down. Examples from MyHealth.Alberta.ca include a warm shower, soothing music, or a cup of herbal tea, as well as meditation or other relaxation techniques. You do not need an elaborate ritual. Ten or twenty unhurried minutes is enough to start.
You might dim the lights, put tomorrow’s clothes where you can find them, write down a worry so it does not have to stay in your head, and then do one calming thing you actually enjoy. The point is repetition, not perfection.
A note about tea and natural health products
A warm cup can be a comforting part of an evening, and herbal tea appears in MyHealth.Alberta.ca’s examples of a relaxing routine. That does not mean a tea treats insomnia, anxiety or any other condition. It is a beverage that some people find soothing, in the same way a warm shower can feel soothing.
Black and green tea contain caffeine. Health Canada’s average figures put brewed black or green tea at about 30 to 50 milligrams of caffeine in a 237 millilitre cup, so an evening “tea” is not automatically caffeine-free. If you want a drink without caffeine, choose a product that says it is caffeine-free and read the label.
If a packaged tea or supplement makes a health claim — for example, that it is for sleep — look for an eight-digit Natural Product Number (NPN) or Homeopathic Medicine Number (DIN-HM) on the label. Health Canada uses that number to show the product has been licensed for sale and assessed for use as directed. Read the purpose, dose and warnings on the label. Talk with a pharmacist or other healthcare provider before you use a natural health product if you are pregnant, trying to become pregnant, breastfeeding, giving a product to a child, or taking other medicines. “Natural” does not mean a product is risk-free or that it will not interact with a medicine.
Do not replace a prescribed sleep medicine, or any other prescribed medicine, with a tea or supplement unless the clinician who prescribed it has agreed.
Caffeine, alcohol and nicotine
MyHealth.Alberta.ca advises avoiding or limiting caffeine, nicotine and alcohol, and not using them late in the day or in the evening. Caffeine is a stimulant. Health Canada notes that it can be linked with insomnia, irritability, headaches and nervousness, and that people who are sensitive to it may want to lower their intake or avoid it.
For most healthy adults, Health Canada’s recommended maximum is 400 milligrams of caffeine a day. That is a total from all sources, not only coffee. The recommended maximum is 300 milligrams a day for people who are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Children and adolescents have a lower, weight-based suggested limit.
Alcohol can make you feel sleepy at first and still interfere with how restful the night feels. If you drink, leaving a longer gap before bed is a gentler habit than using alcohol as a way to fall asleep. Nicotine is also a stimulant, so an evening cigarette or vape can work against the wind-down you are trying to build.
When a routine is not enough
Some people who have ongoing insomnia benefit from a structured approach called cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I). MyHealth.Alberta.ca describes CBT-I as a way to change thoughts and behaviours that get in the way of sleep, and notes that a healthcare provider can recommend specific steps. Some people also take medicine for a time. Those decisions belong in a clinical conversation, not in an article.
A wind-down is a kindness you can offer yourself. It is not a promise of eight unbroken hours, and it is not a substitute for care when sleep trouble is persistent, sudden or paired with other worrying symptoms.

To take with you
Practical takeaways

A wind-down is an everyday routine, not a treatment for insomnia or any other condition.
A regular bedtime and rising time, and using the bed mainly for sleep and sex, are common public-health suggestions.
If you are still awake after about 15 to 20 minutes, get up and do something quiet until you feel sleepy.
Black and green tea contain caffeine. If a packaged product makes a sleep-related claim, look for an NPN or DIN-HM and read the warnings.
Health Canada’s recommended caffeine maximum is 400 milligrams a day for most healthy adults, and 300 milligrams a day if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.



Care in Alberta
When to see a healthcare provider
Talk with a healthcare provider if trouble sleeping is frequent, has lasted more than a few weeks, started after a new medicine, or comes with loud snoring, pauses in breathing, gasping, restless legs, low mood, or other new symptoms. A provider may discuss options such as cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia. Do not start or stop a sleep medicine on your own.
If you are in immediate danger, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department. Bloom does not provide urgent or emergency care. For non-urgent health advice in Alberta, call Health Link at 811, any time. If you or someone you know is thinking about suicide, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide Crisis Helpline, available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.

/library/balanced-eating-made-simple.htm:
Healthy eating does not have to mean a new set of rules every January, or a plate that looks nothing like the food you already enjoy. Canada’s food guide is built around a simple picture: half vegetables and fruits, one-quarter whole grain foods, and one-quarter protein foods, with water as the drink of choice. You can use those proportions as a guide whether supper is on a plate, in a bowl, in a lunch box or shared from a pot.
This article is general information about that pattern. It is not a meal plan, a weight-loss program or nutrition therapy for a medical condition. If you have a condition that affects what you can eat, or if eating itself has become stressful, a regulated healthcare provider can help you find advice that fits you. In Alberta, a Registered Dietitian is a regulated health professional; a nutrition specialist or herbalist is not a substitute for that kind of medical or dietetic care.
Start with the plate, not with perfection
Canada’s food guide suggests making vegetables and fruits the largest part of what you eat through the day — about half of a meal or snack. One-quarter of the plate is whole grain foods, such as whole grain bread, whole grain pasta, brown rice, wild rice or quinoa. The remaining quarter is protein foods. The guide encourages choosing protein foods that come from plants more often.
The pictures on the official plate are examples, not a shopping list you must copy, and they are not meant to show an exact serving size. Fresh, frozen, canned and dried foods can all count. That matters in a Canadian winter, when a bag of frozen peas or a tin of lentils may be the most practical choice on a Tuesday night.
Canada’s dietary guidelines also note that nutritious foods can reflect cultural preferences and food traditions, and that eating with other people can be part of healthy eating. The pattern is meant to flex around the foods you already know and like.
Vegetables and fruits as the larger half
Think of colour and variety over the week rather than a perfect tally at every sitting. Leftover roasted carrots beside a bowl of lentils, berries on oatmeal, a handful of cherry tomatoes with hummus and crackers, or extra peppers stirred into a soup all move a meal toward that larger half.
If you use canned vegetables or fruits, compare labels and look for products with little to no added sodium or sugars when you can. Frozen vegetables without sauce are often a straightforward choice. Dried fruit can belong with a meal; Health Canada notes that it is sticky and can cling to teeth, so it is better eaten with meals than sipped or snacked on all afternoon.
Whole grain foods
Whole grain foods include the entire grain. They can be as everyday as oatmeal, brown rice, whole grain bread or barley in a soup. If you are choosing a packaged grain product, the ingredients list is helpful: the first ingredients tell you what the food contains most of, by weight.
You do not need to abandon foods you love. A familiar pasta night can still follow the plate if half the bowl is vegetables and a quarter is a protein food such as beans, lentils or tofu.
Protein foods, with plants more often
Canada’s dietary guidelines say that among protein foods, plant-based choices should be eaten more often. Health Canada’s kitchen guidance names many of those foods: beans, lentils, chickpeas, tofu, tempeh, nuts, seeds, nut butters and unsweetened fortified soy beverages.
A few everyday swaps illustrate the idea without turning supper into a project: lentils in a chilli, chickpeas tossed through a salad, peanut butter on apple slices, or tofu in a stir-fry that is already half vegetables.
Mixed dishes still follow the same idea
Most home cooking is mixed together. Canada’s food guide says you can still use the plate as a reference for soups, stir-fries, casseroles and other combined dishes by thinking about the proportions going into the pot. For a stir-fry, that might mean plenty of vegetables, a protein food such as tofu or chickpeas, and a whole grain such as brown rice on the side or mixed through.
The same thinking works for breakfast. Oatmeal with enough berries and chopped fruit to fill half the bowl, or toast with peanut butter and apple slices, both follow the same proportions.
What you drink matters too
Health Canada recommends making water your drink of choice. Water quenches thirst and helps you stay hydrated without adding calories. Other everyday options include unsweetened fortified soy beverage, and unsweetened coffee and tea.
Drinks to have less often include sugary drinks, alcoholic drinks, some vegetable juices, and specialty coffees or teas that are high in added sugar or saturated fat. For a child younger than two, a plant beverage is not a suitable main drink. Infants and toddlers need the feeding plan their own clinician has recommended.
Using the nutrition facts table
When you compare packaged foods, Canada’s food guide suggests three steps. First, notice the serving size — the numbers on the table are for that amount, which may not match what you actually eat. Second, use the % daily value: 5% or less is a little, and 15% or more is a lot. Third, read the ingredients list, which is written in order of weight.
When you are choosing between two similar products, look for ones with less sodium, less sugars and less saturated fat. Nutrients many people want more of, such as fibre, iron, calcium and potassium, are often found in vegetables, fruits and other foods that may not even carry a table.
Cooking more often, in a way that fits your life
Cooking more often can make it easier to choose vegetables, fruits, whole grains and protein foods, and to rely a little less on highly processed foods. It also lets you control sauces and seasonings. That does not mean every meal must be cooked from scratch on the day you eat it.
Health Canada’s practical ideas include cooking once and eating twice, batch-cooking soups and stews, and keeping handy ingredients such as canned beans, frozen vegetables, lower-sodium vegetable broth, and herbs and spices. Methods that need little added fat — roasting, steaming, baking, grilling or stir-frying — are useful tools, not rules you have to follow every night.
Healthy eating is a pattern over time. One hurried sandwich does not undo a week of meals you felt good about, and one carefully composed plate does not need to carry the whole story of your health.

To take with you
Practical takeaways

Canada’s food guide uses a simple picture: half vegetables and fruits, one-quarter whole grain foods and one-quarter protein foods.
Choose protein foods that come from plants more often, such as beans, lentils, tofu, nuts and seeds.
Fresh, frozen, canned and dried foods can all fit. Use the plate as a guide for soups, bowls and other mixed dishes too.
Make water your drink of choice. When you compare packaged foods, 5% daily value or less is a little and 15% or more is a lot.
Healthy eating is a pattern over time, not a perfect plate at every meal.



Care in Alberta
When to see a healthcare provider
Talk with a regulated healthcare provider if you have a medical condition that affects what you can eat, if you have lost or gained weight without trying, if swallowing is difficult, or if thoughts about food or eating feel hard to manage. In Alberta, a Registered Dietitian is a regulated health professional who provides nutrition therapy. A nutrition specialist or herbalist is not a substitute for that care.
If you are in immediate danger, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department. Bloom does not provide urgent or emergency care. For non-urgent health advice in Alberta, call Health Link at 811, any time. If you or someone you know is thinking about suicide, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide Crisis Helpline, available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.

/library/hydration-made-easy.html:
Drinking enough can sound like another chore on a long list. Canada’s food guide takes a gentler starting point: make water your drink of choice. Water helps you stay hydrated without adding calories, and it is one of the simplest public health habits to practise at home, at work or on the go.
This article is about everyday drinking habits. It is not a treatment plan for dehydration or for any medical condition, and it does not give a single number of glasses that everyone should finish each day. How much fluid a person needs varies.
Why water comes first
Our bodies lose water by sweating, breathing and getting rid of waste. That water needs to be replaced. Health Canada recommends water as the beverage of choice because it supports health and hydration without adding calories to the diet. Water is essential for ordinary metabolic and digestive processes, and it is the largest single component of the human body.
Canada’s dietary guidelines note that most people consume enough total water to meet their hydration needs, and that total water includes fluids from food as well as from drinks. Fruit, vegetables and soups all contribute. Physical activity and hot weather can increase how much you need. Young children and older adults are among those most at risk of becoming dehydrated.
Some communities in Canada, including some remote, isolated and northern communities, do not always have ready access to safe drinking water. If a drinking water advisory is in place where you live, follow local public health instructions.
Easy ways to drink more water
Canada’s food guide offers everyday tactics rather than a rigid schedule:

Drink water with your meals, hot or cold.
Keep a pitcher of water in the fridge or on the table so it is the drink you see first.
Carry a reusable bottle when you are out.
Ask for water when you eat in a restaurant.
Drink water during and after physical activity.
Try carbonated water if you like a little fizz, or add fruit and herbs if plain water bores you.

Pairing water with something you already do — sitting down at the computer, leaving the house, finishing a walk — is often easier than trying to remember “one more glass” in the abstract.
If you like a little flavour
Health Canada suggests adding fruit and herbs to hot or cold water. Official combinations to try include blackberries with mint, raspberries with cucumber, strawberries with fresh basil, chopped apples with a cinnamon stick, and pear slices with a drop of vanilla extract. Crushing berries, chopping or tearing herbs, and cutting fruit into cubes helps more flavour come through.
Lemon in water is a taste preference, not a cleanse or a medical treatment. Infused water is still water. If you add commercial flavour drops or powders, read the label for sugars and sodium.
Other drinks that can fit
Water does not have to be your only drink. Unsweetened fortified soy beverage, and unsweetened coffee and tea, can fit alongside water for many adults. For a child younger than two, a plant beverage is not a suitable main drink. Infants and toddlers need the feeding plan their own clinician has recommended.
Drinks to have less often include sugary drinks, alcoholic drinks, some vegetable juices, and specialty coffees or teas that are high in added sugar or saturated fat. When you compare packaged drinks, the nutrition facts table can help you choose ones that are lower in those nutrients. As a reading guide, 5% daily value or less is a little, and 15% or more is a lot.
A word about caffeine
Caffeine occurs naturally in coffee, tea, chocolate and some other plants, and it is added to some foods and drinks. It is a stimulant. Health Canada notes that it may be linked with insomnia, irritability, headaches and nervousness, and that it affects children more than adults because children have smaller body weights.
For most healthy adults, Health Canada’s recommended maximum is 400 milligrams of caffeine a day from all sources. The recommended maximum is 300 milligrams a day for people who are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. An average 237 millilitre cup of brewed coffee has about 135 milligrams of caffeine; the same amount of brewed black or green tea has about 30 to 50 milligrams. If you are sensitive to caffeine, consider having less or avoiding it, especially later in the day if sleep matters to you.
Unsweetened coffee and tea can still fit as drinks you enjoy. They are not a replacement for water, and energy drinks or specialty coffees can add sugars and a large amount of caffeine without looking like “just a coffee.”
Who may need to pay closer attention
MyHealth.Alberta.ca notes that dehydration can happen at any age when you stop drinking enough, or when you lose a lot of fluid through diarrhea, vomiting, sweating or exercise. It is most dangerous for babies, small children and older adults.
Older adults may not feel thirsty even when they need fluids. Other reasons include kidneys that do not work as well, medicines that increase urine (such as some blood pressure medicines, diuretics or antihistamines), trouble reaching a drink or the toilet, or drinking less because of bladder concerns.
If you have a health condition, or if you take medicines that affect fluid balance, ask your healthcare provider how those facts change everyday drinking for you. Do not make large, sudden changes to fluid intake because of something you read, especially if you have been told to limit fluids.
Early signs that you may be getting dehydrated
MyHealth.Alberta.ca lists early symptoms that can include a mouth and eyes that are drier than usual, passing less urine than usual, and feeling cranky, tired or dizzy. Mild dehydration may mean you are more thirsty than usual and passing less urine. Moderate dehydration may mean much more thirst, a drier mouth and eyes, little or no urine for 8 or more hours, or dizziness when you stand or sit up.
Severe dehydration is an emergency. Warning signs can include a mouth and eyes that are extremely dry, little or no urine for 12 or more hours, trouble thinking clearly or staying alert, feeling too weak or dizzy to stand, or passing out. Call 911 or go to an emergency department if you think you or someone you are with may have severe dehydration or shock.
For milder questions — for example, after a stomach illness, or if you are not sure whether you are keeping enough down — call Health Link at 811 or contact a healthcare provider. Do not rely on an herbal product, a specialty drink or a “hydration supplement” to treat dehydration. If a packaged product makes a health claim, look for an eight-digit Natural Product Number (NPN) or Homeopathic Medicine Number (DIN-HM) and read the warnings, then ask a pharmacist or other provider whether it is appropriate for you.

To take with you
Practical takeaways

Canada’s food guide recommends making water your drink of choice. There is no single number of glasses that fits everyone.
Keep water visible: a pitcher on the table, a bottle in your bag, and water with meals.
Fruit-and-herb infusions are for flavour, not as a cleanse or treatment.
For most healthy adults, Health Canada’s recommended caffeine maximum is 400 milligrams a day, and 300 milligrams if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
Babies, young children and older adults can become dehydrated more easily. Early signs can include a drier mouth, less urine than usual, tiredness or dizziness.



Care in Alberta
When to see a healthcare provider
Contact a healthcare provider or call Health Link at 811 if you cannot keep fluids down, if you are passing much less urine than usual, or if you are caring for a baby, young child or older adult and are worried about fluids. Ask your provider before making large changes to how much you drink if you have been told to limit fluids or if you take medicines that affect fluid balance.
Severe dehydration is an emergency. Call 911 or go to an emergency department if a mouth and eyes are extremely dry, if there is little or no urine for 12 or more hours, if someone cannot think clearly or stay alert, cannot stand because of weakness or dizziness, or passes out. Bloom does not provide urgent or emergency care. If you or someone you know is thinking about suicide, call or text 988.

/library/understanding-your-blood-work.h:
A laboratory report can look like a second language: short names, units and a column of numbers beside a “normal” range. This guide explains what several common blood tests measure, how you may be asked to prepare, and how to use the report as a starting point for a conversation. It cannot tell you what your own results mean, and it is not a diagnosis. Your results belong in the wider story of your health — how you feel, the medicines and products you take, and what else is going on in your life.
Blood work is one part of the picture
Healthcare providers order blood tests to look into symptoms such as fatigue, weakness, fever, bruising or weight change; to screen for certain conditions; to see how a medicine is agreeing with you; or to keep an eye on something you already know about.
No single number stands alone. MyHealth.Alberta.ca notes that each laboratory has its own range for what it calls normal, that the range is only a guide, and that a value outside that range may still be typical for you. Age, sex, pregnancy, other health conditions and even how much fluid is in your body can all shape a result.
How to prepare for common tests
Preparation is not the same for every test, so use the instructions from the laboratory or the clinician who ordered the work.

A complete blood count usually needs no special preparation.
A fasting blood glucose test typically means no food or drink other than water for at least 8 hours beforehand.
For cholesterol and triglyceride tests, you may be asked not to eat or drink anything except water for 9 to 14 hours. Fasting is not always required, but it may be recommended. MyHealth.Alberta.ca also advises not drinking alcohol for 24 hours before those tests.
A ferritin test usually needs no special steps unless you are told otherwise.
If you take thyroid medicine, say when you took your last dose. You may be asked to pause it for a short time before thyroid hormone testing.
Creatinine can read temporarily higher after a very large high-protein meal, intense exercise, or some supplements such as creatine, so mention these to your provider and follow any prep instructions you're given.

Tell the person ordering the test about all medicines and natural health products you take. Some products can affect a result. If you use a natural health product, look for an eight-digit Natural Product Number (NPN) or Homeopathic Medicine Number (DIN-HM) on the label, which means Health Canada has licensed it for sale when it is used as directed.
A complete blood count (CBC)
A CBC looks at the kinds and numbers of cells in your blood — especially red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets. Red blood cells carry oxygen from the lungs through the body. Hemoglobin is the protein inside those cells that carries oxygen and gives blood its colour. Hematocrit describes how much of the blood’s volume is made up of red cells. Low values may point toward anemia, which has many possible causes. High values can have other explanations, including how much fluid is in the body at the time of the test.
White blood cells help the body respond to infection. Their total number, and the mix of different types, can offer clues about infection, inflammation or a reaction to a medicine. Platelets help blood clot. Too few or too many can matter for bleeding or clotting. Only a clinician can put those numbers in context. A blood draw usually feels like a brief sting or pinch; a small bruise at the site is common, and serious problems from the draw itself are uncommon.
Blood glucose and the A1C test
A blood glucose test measures sugar in the blood. A fasting blood sugar is taken after you have not eaten for at least 8 hours and is often used as an early check for prediabetes or diabetes. A random blood sugar can be taken without that waiting period.
The A1C test (also called hemoglobin A1C) shows the average level of blood sugar over about the past 2 to 3 months. It may be used to help diagnose diabetes or prediabetes, or to see how glucose has been running over time. It is not the right test for everyone. Pregnancy in the second or third trimester, a recent blood loss or transfusion, sickle cell disease, hemodialysis and some medicines that affect red blood cells can all change how the result should be read. If you have questions about a glucose or A1C result, review them with a regulated healthcare provider rather than trying to interpret them on your own.
Cholesterol and triglycerides
Cholesterol and triglyceride tests measure fats, often called lipids. A typical report may include total cholesterol, triglycerides, HDL cholesterol (often called “good” cholesterol) and LDL cholesterol (often called “bad” cholesterol).
Providers may use these results with other information — such as blood pressure, whether you have diabetes, your age and sex, and whether you smoke — when they talk about heart and blood-vessel risk. The numbers alone do not tell the whole story, and they are not a reason to start or stop a medicine on your own.
Thyroid hormone tests
The thyroid is a small gland in the front of the neck that makes hormones to help regulate how the body uses energy. Blood tests may measure thyroxine (T4), including free T4, and triiodothyronine (T3), often to help explain a thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) result or to follow treatment that has already been started.
Many things can change thyroid hormone levels. A clinician will talk with you about unusual results in light of your symptoms and past health. Everyday foods, teas or supplements should not be used to treat a thyroid number you see on a report.
Ferritin, and how much iron you have stored
Ferritin is a protein that binds iron, and the amount in the blood is used as a window onto iron stored in the body. The test may be ordered to look into anemia, inflammation, too much stored iron, or how iron treatment is going. Low ferritin often points toward low iron stores, which can follow blood loss, pregnancy or too little iron in the diet. High ferritin can have many causes as well. Either result is a starting point for a conversation, not a plan to carry out on your own.
Creatinine and how the kidneys filter waste
Creatinine is a waste product formed when creatine — made when food is turned into energy — is broken down. Healthy kidneys remove creatinine from the blood and pass it out in urine. A blood creatinine level is one way to look at how the kidneys are working. If they are not filtering as they should, creatinine in the blood may rise. The amount also depends partly on muscle mass, so men often have higher levels than women. Dehydration, some medicines, diet and muscle injury can all influence the number.
How to read the numbers on your report
Most reports list the test name, your result, the units and the laboratory’s reference interval. Flags such as “H” or “L” only mean the number sits outside that printed range. They do not tell you how important the finding is or what to do next. Resist matching a single flagged result to a condition you have read about online, or to a supplement that claims to correct a lab value. If a packaged natural health product makes a health claim, check that it has an NPN or DIN-HM. Even then, a licensed product is not a personal treatment plan.
Questions that can help at your next visit
You might write down a few of these before you sit down with your provider:

Why was this test ordered for me?
Did I need to fast or change any medicines beforehand, and did that go as planned?
Which results matter most in my situation, and which ones are you not concerned about?
Could anything else — including pregnancy, recent illness, dehydration, or a medicine or natural health product — have influenced the numbers?
Do I need another test, a different kind of test, or a follow-up visit?
What symptoms should prompt me to get in touch sooner?

You can always ask for an explanation in everyday language, and you can ask for time to think before you decide on next steps.

To take with you
Practical takeaways

Blood tests are one tool. Your healthcare provider reads them alongside your symptoms, medicines, health history and physical findings.
Preparation depends on the test. A complete blood count usually needs no special steps, while some glucose and cholesterol tests may require fasting. Follow the instructions you are given.
Each laboratory prints its own reference range on the report. A number outside that range may still be typical for you.
Bring a written list of questions, and a list of your medicines and natural health products, to your results visit.
Do not start, stop or change a medicine or supplement because of a number you see on a report. Review the results with a regulated healthcare provider first.



Care in Alberta
When to see a healthcare provider
Book a visit with a nurse practitioner, physician or other regulated healthcare provider if you have new or unexplained symptoms, if you have been asked to review results and are not sure what they mean, or if you want help deciding whether testing is right for you.
Seek urgent care if you have symptoms such as chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, sudden weakness, confusion, or heavy bleeding that you cannot control. Bloom does not provide urgent or emergency care.
If you are in immediate danger, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department. For non-urgent health advice in Alberta, call Health Link at 811, any time. If you or someone you know is thinking about suicide, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide Crisis Helpline, available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.

/library/warming-winter-soups.html:
A pot of soup is one of the gentler ways to cook in cold weather. It can also follow the shape of Canada’s food guide: plenty of vegetables, a protein food, and a whole grain on the side or stirred through. This page shares three simple recipes and some practical notes on flavour, leftovers and food safety. It is not a treatment for a cold, the flu or any other illness, and no soup here is offered as a way to prevent or cure a disease.
Canada’s food guide treats mixed dishes such as soups as meals you can still “plate” in your mind. Aim for vegetables to make up about half of what goes into the pot, add a protein food such as beans, lentils or tofu, and serve a whole grain — barley in the soup, or whole grain bread on the side — as about a quarter of the meal. Water, or the soup itself, can help with everyday fluids. Health Canada also notes that water from foods such as vegetables and soups contributes to overall fluid intake.
Flavour without leaning only on salt
Soup can hide a lot of sodium, especially if it starts with a salty broth or canned ingredients. Canada’s food guide encourages choosing foods with little to no added sodium, sugars or saturated fat, and using the nutrition facts table to compare products. As a quick reading guide, 5% daily value or less is a little, and 15% or more is a lot.
A few habits help you keep flavour while going easier on the salt:

Choose a lower-sodium vegetable broth, or use water plus herbs and spices and add salt at the end only if you need it.
Rinse canned beans or lentils under water before they go in the pot.
Build flavour with onion, garlic, celery, bay, thyme, pepper, lemon, vinegar or parsley.
Taste before you salt. A squeeze of lemon at the table often brightens a soup more than another pinch of salt would.

Cooking a pot yourself also lets you control sauces and seasonings, which is one reason Health Canada encourages cooking more often.
Three simple soups
Each recipe makes about four servings, depending on appetite. Times are estimates. Use what you have: frozen vegetables are welcome, and extra canned beans can stand in where noted. If you cook for someone with allergies, read every label and skip or replace ingredients as needed.

Root vegetable and red lentil soup
About 4 servings · About 45 minutes
Red lentils soften as they cook and give the soup a gentle body, so it does not need a thickener. This is a good place to use the pale winter vegetables that keep well in a Canadian kitchen.
You will need

15 mL (1 tablespoon) olive oil or canola oil
1 onion, chopped
2 carrots, chopped
2 celery stalks, chopped
1 parsnip or small sweet potato, chopped
2 garlic cloves, minced
15 mL (1 tablespoon) tomato paste
5 mL (1 teaspoon) ground cumin
2 mL (½ teaspoon) dried thyme
250 mL (1 cup) dry red lentils, rinsed
1.5 L (6 cups) lower-sodium vegetable broth or water
Pepper, and lemon wedges to serve

Method

Warm the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Cook the onion, carrots, celery and parsnip, stirring now and then, until the onion looks soft, about 8 minutes.
Stir in the garlic, tomato paste, cumin and thyme for one minute.
Add the lentils and broth. Bring to a gentle boil, then lower the heat and simmer, partly covered, until the lentils and vegetables are tender, about 20 minutes. Add a splash of water if the soup becomes thicker than you like.
Season with pepper. For a smoother texture, mash some of the soup with a spoon or blend part of it. Serve with lemon and, if you like, a slice of whole grain bread.



White bean, cabbage and rosemary soup
About 4 servings · About 40 minutes
Cabbage and canned white beans make a filling pot without much fuss. Rosemary is used here as a kitchen herb for flavour, not as a herbal medicine.
You will need

15 mL (1 tablespoon) olive oil or canola oil
1 onion, chopped
2 carrots, chopped
2 garlic cloves, minced
5 mL (1 teaspoon) chopped fresh rosemary, or 2 mL (½ teaspoon) dried
1 L (4 cups) chopped green cabbage
1 can (540 mL / 19 oz) white beans, drained and rinsed
1.25 L (5 cups) lower-sodium vegetable broth
15 mL (1 tablespoon) lemon juice or apple cider vinegar
Pepper, and chopped parsley if you have it

Method

Warm the oil in a large pot. Cook the onion and carrots until they begin to soften, about 7 minutes. Stir in the garlic and rosemary for one minute.
Add the cabbage, beans and broth. Bring to a boil, then simmer until the cabbage is tender, about 15 to 20 minutes.
Stir in the lemon juice or vinegar. Taste, add pepper, and finish with parsley. Whole grain toast on the side turns this into an easy supper.



Chickpea and barley pot
About 4 servings · About 55 minutes
Barley is a whole grain, and chickpeas add protein, so the pot is hearty enough to be dinner.
You will need

15 mL (1 tablespoon) olive oil or canola oil
1 onion, chopped
2 carrots, chopped
2 celery stalks, chopped
150 g (¾ cup) pot or pearl barley, rinsed
1.5 L (6 cups) lower-sodium vegetable broth
1 bay leaf
2 mL (½ teaspoon) dried thyme
250 mL (1 cup) frozen peas or green beans
1 can (540 mL) chickpeas, drained and rinsed
Pepper and parsley

Method

Warm the oil in a large pot. Cook the onion, carrots and celery until the onion is soft, about 8 minutes.
Stir in the barley, then add the broth, bay leaf and thyme. Bring to a boil, then simmer until the barley is tender, about 30 to 40 minutes. Add water if you need to.
Stir in the peas or green beans and the chickpeas. Cook another 5 minutes, until everything is hot. Remove the bay leaf, add pepper and parsley, and serve.


Storing and reheating leftovers safely
Health Canada’s leftover guidance is worth following with soup, because a large pot cools slowly.

Keep food out of the temperature “danger zone” between 4°C (40°F) and 60°C (140°F), where harmful bacteria can grow more easily.
Throw away any cooked food left at room temperature for more than two hours. If the air is hotter than 32°C (90°F), do not leave cooked food out for more than one hour. Do not rely on smell or taste to decide whether leftover food is safe.
Refrigerate leftovers promptly in uncovered, shallow containers so they cool quickly. Very hot soup can sit until it stops steaming, then go into the fridge. Leave the lid loose until the soup is cold.
Eat refrigerated leftovers within 2 to 3 days, or freeze them. Dating the container helps.
Thaw frozen soup in the refrigerator or in the microwave, then cook or eat it right away.
Reheat leftovers to a safe internal temperature of 74°C (165°F). Bring soups to a full, rolling boil and stir as they heat. Discard any reheated leftover that you do not eat.

If you reheat in a microwave, use a microwave-safe container, loosen the lid so steam can escape, and stir halfway through so the heat spreads evenly.
Making one pot last
Health Canada suggests cooking once and eating twice, and names soups as a good candidate for batch cooking. Freeze some in meal-size portions once the soup has cooled.
Let people add their own finish at the table — pepper, herbs or lemon — so the pot itself can stay quieter on salt.

To take with you
Practical takeaways

Use Canada’s food guide as a guide for soup: plenty of vegetables, a protein food, and a whole grain in the pot or on the side.
Compare broths and canned foods with the nutrition facts table. Five percent daily value or less is a little sodium; 15% or more is a lot.
Refrigerate leftovers promptly in shallow containers, eat them within 2 to 3 days or freeze them, and reheat soup to a full rolling boil (74°C / 165°F).
Throw away cooked food left at room temperature for more than two hours, or one hour if it is hotter than 32°C (90°F). When in doubt, throw it out.
These recipes are everyday meals, not remedies for colds or other illnesses.



Care in Alberta
When to see a healthcare provider
Call a healthcare provider or Health Link at 811 if you think you have food poisoning and symptoms are severe or lasting, if you cannot keep fluids down, or if you have a condition that makes foodborne illness more risky. Seek urgent care if you have signs of severe dehydration, bloody stool, a high fever, or confusion.
If you are in immediate danger, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department. Bloom does not provide urgent or emergency care. If you or someone you know is thinking about suicide, call or text 988.

/library/what-to-expect-at-your-first-vi:
Coming to a first virtual visit can feel like stepping into a house you have not visited before. This page walks through how Bloom appointments are set up, what you can do to prepare, and how medical care and wellness support differ. It is a general description of our services. Your own visit will depend on what you hope to discuss and on the professional judgment of the person you see.
Because our Nurse Practitioners are licensed in Alberta, you need to be in Alberta during each virtual appointment. We are a private clinic in Calgary. We do not provide urgent or emergency care.
The visits Bloom offers
You can book one of three visits. Prices are in Canadian dollars.

A medical visit with a Nurse Practitioner is 30 minutes and costs $195.
A wellness visit with a Herbalist and Nutrition Specialist is 30 minutes and costs $135.
An integrated visit is 60 minutes with the Nurse Practitioner and the Herbalist & Nutrition Specialist together. It costs $330.

Prices do not include GST, where applicable.
Appointments are currently offered Monday to Friday, from 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. If you would like to be contacted when a time is available, you can join the waitlist. Joining the waitlist does not guarantee an appointment and does not create a practitioner–client relationship.
Your Nurse Practitioner visit
Medical visits at Bloom are provided by Iris Calloway, MN, NP. A Nurse Practitioner is a regulated health professional. In Alberta, Nurse Practitioners practise under the standards of the College of Registered Nurses of Alberta (CRNA). The title to use is Nurse Practitioner, or NP. Please do not use the title “doctor.”
A medical visit may include talking through your health history and current concerns, reviewing medicines and relevant test results, and discussing possible next steps. Depending on your situation, that might include laboratory work or other investigations, a prescription if one is appropriate, or a suggestion to follow up in person or with another service. A Nurse Practitioner works within their professional scope. A first visit cannot cover every issue, and not every concern can be safely assessed by video.
What happens in your visit is individual. No article can promise a particular diagnosis, prescription, test or outcome.
Your Herbalist and Nutrition Specialist visit
Wellness visits at Bloom are offered by Rosemary Hale, Herbalist and Nutrition Specialist. This is complementary wellness support: education and coaching around everyday habits, food and herbal products. It is not medical care, and it does not replace an assessment by a Nurse Practitioner, physician, Registered Dietitian or other regulated health professional.
Herbalists and nutrition specialists are not a regulated health profession in Alberta. Rosemary Hale is not a Registered Dietitian, a physician or a Nurse Practitioner, and a wellness visit is not a medical diagnosis or a medical treatment. If a food, tea or natural health product comes up in conversation, that discussion is educational. Any product that makes a health claim in Canada should carry an eight-digit Natural Product Number (NPN) or Homeopathic Medicine Number (DIN-HM) on the label. “Natural” does not mean a product is suitable for you, free of side effects, or safe to mix with medicines.
If you are pregnant, trying to become pregnant, breastfeeding, giving a product to a child, or taking other medicines, ask a pharmacist or other healthcare provider before you start a natural health product.
If you book an integrated visit
An integrated visit is one 60-minute appointment with your Nurse Practitioner and your Herbalist & Nutrition Specialist. It brings medical care and wellness support together in a single appointment.
The Nurse Practitioner remains responsible for medical assessment, diagnoses, prescriptions and decisions about tests. The Herbalist & Nutrition Specialist offers complementary wellness education and coaching. That support does not replace medical care, and it does not turn wellness guidance into a medical treatment.
How to prepare
A little preparation helps your visit time go further:

Find a private place with a stable internet connection, and test your camera and microphone ahead of time if you can.
Have your government-issued identification nearby if you are asked to confirm who you are.
Write down your main questions. If you have several, put the most important one first.
Make a list of medicines, vitamins and natural health products you take, including doses if you know them. Keep the bottles nearby so you can read the labels.
If you have recent laboratory reports or clinic letters, have them available to look at or share as instructed.
Note any allergies, and the name of the pharmacy you usually use.
Join a few minutes early so technical hiccups are less likely to use up visit time.

During the visit
Your practitioner will ask questions and give you time to describe what has been going on. You can say if you do not understand something, if you need a moment, or if you would rather not discuss a topic. You can also ask what will happen after the visit, including how any follow-up, prescriptions or suggested tests will be handled.
A virtual visit has limits. If the person you are seeing decides that you need an in-person examination, urgent care or another service, they should say so. You should also say if you feel worse during the visit or if you think you need emergency care.
After the visit, billing and prescriptions
Our clinic does not offer direct billing for visits or services. Our partner pharmacy can direct bill your insurance for prescribed medications and supplies, and can check your coverage for you. You pay for the appointment, and you can submit the receipt to your insurer yourself if you have coverage. Whether a visit is reimbursed depends on your plan.
Canadian rules limit how prescription medicines may be advertised to the public, so this page does not name or promote any prescription drug. A prescription is written only after a real assessment in a visit. An article cannot do that.
Cancellations and changing your time
If you need to cancel or reschedule, please let us know at least 24 hours before your appointment. You will receive a full refund, or we will move you to a new time. Cancellations or changes made within 24 hours of the appointment, and missed appointments, are charged the full visit fee.
If you need care sooner than a booked visit
Bloom does not provide urgent or emergency care, and booking or joining the waitlist is not a way to get immediate help. If you are in immediate danger, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department. For non-urgent advice, call Health Link at 811.

To take with you
Practical takeaways

Because our Nurse Practitioners are licensed in Alberta, you need to be in Alberta during each virtual appointment. A 30-minute medical visit is $195, a 30-minute wellness visit is $135, and a 60-minute integrated visit is $330. Prices do not include GST, where applicable.
Medical visits are provided by Iris Calloway, MN, NP. In Alberta, Nurse Practitioners practise under the standards of the College of Registered Nurses of Alberta. The title to use is Nurse Practitioner, or NP, not “doctor.”
Wellness visits with Rosemary Hale, Herbalist and Nutrition Specialist, are complementary education and coaching. They are not medical care and do not replace a regulated health professional.
An integrated visit is one 60-minute appointment with the Nurse Practitioner and the Herbalist & Nutrition Specialist. It brings medical care and wellness support together in one appointment. A prescription is written only after an assessment.
Our clinic does not offer direct billing for visits or services. Our partner pharmacy can direct bill your insurance for prescribed medications and supplies, and can check your coverage for you. Cancel or reschedule at least 24 hours ahead for a full refund or a new time.



Care in Alberta
When to see a healthcare provider
Bloom does not provide urgent or emergency care. If a concern cannot wait for a booked virtual visit — for example chest pain, trouble breathing, severe bleeding, fainting, sudden confusion, thoughts of harming yourself, or a child who is very unwell — call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department.
For non-urgent health advice in Alberta, call Health Link at 811, any time. If you or someone you know is thinking about suicide, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide Crisis Helpline, available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.
